name: git config
shortDescription: Get and set repository or global configuration options. This is how you tell Git who you are, how you want it to behave, and customize your workflow.
detailedDescription:
Git configuration is stored at three levels, each overriding the one above it:

1. **System** (`/etc/gitconfig`) — applies to every user on the machine. Rarely modified.
2. **Global** (`~/.gitconfig`) — applies to your user account across all repositories. This is where you set your name, email, and preferred editor.
3. **Local** (`.git/config`) — applies only to the current repository. Overrides global settings.

The `git config` command reads and writes these files. The most critical settings are `user.name` and `user.email`, which are embedded in every commit you make. If these aren't set, Git will refuse to commit (or use system defaults that may be wrong).

Beyond identity, `git config` controls aliases, merge strategies, diff tools, color output, line endings, credential caching, and hundreds of other behaviors.

parameters.description: Write to the global config file (~/.gitconfig). Use this for settings that should apply to all your repositories: your name, email, editor, aliases, etc.
Write to the repository-specific config file (.git/config). This is the default when inside a repository.
Write to the system-wide config file (/etc/gitconfig). Requires admin/root privileges. Applies to all users on the machine.
List all configuration variables and their values from all levels, showing which file each setting comes from when combined with --show-origin.
Remove a configuration entry. Useful for reverting a setting back to the default behavior.
When listing or getting config values, show which config file each value comes from. Extremely useful for debugging configuration issues.
Opens the configuration file in your editor for direct editing, rather than setting individual values via command line.

examples.title: Essential first-time setup
examples.description: Every new Git installation needs these two commands. Your name and email are baked into every commit, so set them correctly from the start.
examples.code:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

# Verify your settings:
git config --global --list

examples.title: Set your preferred editor
examples.description: Git opens an editor for commit messages, interactive rebase, etc. Set it to your editor of choice instead of the default (usually vim).
examples.code:
# VS Code
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"

# Nano (simpler than vim)
git config --global core.editor nano

# Sublime Text
git config --global core.editor "subl -n -w"

examples.title: Create powerful aliases
examples.description: Aliases save keystrokes and combine complex commands into simple shortcuts. These are some of the most popular ones in the Git community.
examples.code:
git config --global alias.st status
git config --global alias.co checkout
git config --global alias.br branch
git config --global alias.cm "commit -m"
git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --all --decorate"

# Now you can use:
# git st      → git status
# git lg      → beautiful graph log

examples.title: Fix line-ending issues (Windows/Mac/Linux teams)
examples.description: Cross-platform teams often hit line-ending problems. Configure Git to handle them automatically based on your OS.
examples.code:
# On Windows (converts LF to CRLF on checkout):
git config --global core.autocrlf true

# On macOS/Linux (converts CRLF to LF on commit):
git config --global core.autocrlf input

examples.title: Cache credentials to avoid repeated logins
examples.description: If you use HTTPS and are tired of entering your password every time, enable credential caching.
examples.code:
# Cache for 1 hour (3600 seconds):
git config --global credential.helper 'cache --timeout=3600'

# On macOS, use the Keychain:
git config --global credential.helper osxkeychain

# On Windows, use the Credential Manager:
git config --global credential.helper manager-core

examples.title: Debug: find where a setting comes from
examples.description: When a setting seems wrong and you can't figure out why, --show-origin reveals exactly which config file is responsible.
examples.code:
git config --list --show-origin

# Output shows the file path for each setting:
# file:/Users/you/.gitconfig   user.name=Your Name
# file:.git/config             remote.origin.url=...

commonMistakes.text: Using a wrong email in commits can cause problems: GitHub won't link commits to your profile, company policies may flag commits from personal emails, and changing the email later doesn't fix past commits.
Settings in `.git/config` (local) override `~/.gitconfig` (global). If a setting seems to be ignored, check the local config. Use `git config --list --show-origin` to debug.
Use `git config --global --edit` to open the entire global config file in your editor. It's often faster than setting values one by one when making multiple changes.
